These findings highlight the potential of RL-only training for reasoning enhancement and suggest future work on refining reward structures to bridge emergent insights with accuracy.
provider_summary: [research paper] A 3B language model is trained on the Countdown Game using pure reinforcement learning (RL) without supervised fine-tuning, employing a rule-based reward model that enforces response structure and correctness. The model outperforms baselines on four out of five benchmarks, demonstrating improved generalization beyond training data, while revealing a negative correlation between response length and reasoning quality—longer responses do not imply better reasoning. Emergent 'aha moments' occur but are not consistently linked to correct answers, suggesting that reward design must evolve to align insight with accuracy.
title: Reinforcement Learning is all You Need

abstract: Recent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have shown strong performance in complex domains such as Atari games, but are often highly sample inefficient. A common approach to reduce interaction time with the environment is to use reward shaping, which involves carefully designing reward functions that provide the agent intermediate rewards for progress towards the goal. However, designing appropriate shaping rewards is known to be difficult as well as time-consuming. In this work, we address this problem by using natural language instructions to perform reward shaping. We propose the LanguagE-Action Reward Network (LEARN), a framework that maps free-form natural language instructions to intermediate rewards based on actions taken by the agent. These intermediate language-based rewards can seamlessly be integrated into any standard reinforcement learning algorithm. We experiment with Montezuma's Revenge from the Atari Learning Environment, a popular benchmark in RL. Our experiments on a diverse set of 15 tasks demonstrate that, for the same number of interactions with the environment, language-based rewards lead to successful completion of the task 60% more often on average, compared to learning without language.
provider_summary: [research paper] The paper proposes LEARN, a neural network framework that maps natural language instructions to intermediate rewards by predicting whether an agent's trajectory aligns with the language description. It addresses symbol grounding and instruction ambiguity through action-frequency vectors derived from trajectory segments, enabling dense reward shaping in sparse-reward reinforcement learning. Experiments on Montezuma’s Revenge show 60% higher task success rate with language-based rewards compared to baseline methods, demonstrating robustness to instruction variation and enabling non-experts to guide agent learning.
title: Using Natural Language for Reward Shaping in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), the term self-play describes a kind of multi-agent learning (MAL) that deploys an algorithm against copies of itself to test compatibility in various stochastic environments. As is typical in MAL, the literature draws heavily from well-established concepts in classical game theory and so this survey quickly reviews some fundamental concepts. In what follows, we present a brief survey of self-play literature, its major themes, criteria, and techniques, and then conclude with an assessment of current shortfalls of the literature as well as suggestions for future directions.
provider_summary: This survey analyzes the theoretical foundations and practical limitations of self-play in multi-agent reinforcement learning, identifying key gaps in performance benchmarks, finite-time guarantees, and algorithmic design. It highlights that current self-play algorithms rely on a 'propose-then-adapt' framework, often converging to Nash equilibria without ensuring Pareto efficiency or fairness, and lack robust finite-time regret bounds against non-self players. The paper argues for a shift toward more realistic performance criteria—such as Pareto efficiency and cooperative fairness—and calls for methods that maintain high performance under both self-play and adversarial conditions.
title: Survey of Self-Play in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: For most reinforcement learning approaches, the learning is performed by maximizing an accumulative reward that is expectedly and manually defined for specific tasks. However, in real world, rewards are emergent phenomena from the complex interactions between agents and environments. In this paper, we propose an implicit generic reward model for reinforcement learning. Unlike those rewards that are manually defined for specific tasks, such implicit reward is task independent. It only comes from the deviation from the agents' previous experiences.
provider_summary: [research paper] Proposes an implicit, task-independent reward model in reinforcement learning derived from experience enrichment via unsupervised representation learning. Uses GANs to learn a low-dimensional latent space of past experiences, constructs an inverse mapping to estimate experience density, and defines reward as inverse probability density—higher reward for rare (outlier) experiences. Enables agents to discover intrinsic motivation for exploration and task mastery without explicit reward design, mimicking human curiosity through experience richness.
